problem: 'Thirty years later, as President, he would end another world war': 1918 to 1945 is 27 years.

fix.bio: Truman reenlisted at 33 and took command of a rowdy Irish-Catholic Kansas City battery in July 1918, leading it through the Meuse-Argonne. His letters to his future wife are businesslike, boastful about rounds fired, and contemptuous of the enemy. Twenty-seven years later, as President, he would end another world war.

Cushing did not bury McCrae. He attended McCrae's funeral at Wimereux on 29 January 1918.

fix.bio: The founder of modern neurosurgery spent much of the war at British casualty clearing stations, pioneering techniques for brain wounds (including pulling shell fragments out with a magnet). His journal records the surgeon's eye on the war, and the deaths of friends: his mentor William Osler lost his son Revere, mortally wounded in Flanders in August 1917, and in January 1918 Cushing attended the funeral of the poet John McCrae.

problem: McCrae died at No. 14 General Hospital, Wimereux (near Boulogne), not at Boulogne itself, and was buried at Wimereux.

fix.digest: Cushing records the death of the Canadian physician-poet John McCrae, author of 'In Flanders Fields', from pneumonia and meningitis at No. 14 General Hospital, Wimereux, near Boulogne. He thinks of him as a soldier through and through, and reflects how much McCrae would have hated dying in bed rather than in the field. The next day he describes the burial at Wimereux with military honours.

fix.digest: At a pacifist rally near the Reichstag the speeches are broken off three times by shooting and once by cannon fire; each time the crowd scatters and drifts back. The bio states as fact that 'that night his flotilla fought German destroyers'. Saskatchewan was in an escort group, not a flotilla, and the action and sinkings are only Raymond's claim, as the entry itself notes. 'He later settled in the United States, which is why...' is an inference.

fix.bio: Raymond's destroyer guarded the landing forces rather than carrying them, so his D-Day is seen from the sea: smoke, bombardment, and an ocean full of landing craft. That night, he recorded, his group engaged German destroyers. His diary is now held by the Library of Virginia.

problem: 'That night his flotilla engaged two German destroyers': 'flotilla' should be 'escort group'. The claim is already flagged as his own.

fix.source_note: 'The diaries of Nella Last' (A Narrative of Their Own, Substack), quoting the entry of Thursday 10 May 1945. Pages from January 1944 to early May 1945 are lost (Wikipedia), so there is no VE Day entry.

problem: 'Disease X' is a quoted coinage from dispatches first published in 2005–06. It is a two-word term rather than a sentence, but it falls under the post-1929 publication rule. Render it unquoted.

fix.digest: Writing after midnight, Weller reports that the city's hospitals are still losing patients to a strange effect of the bomb. People who thought they had escaped are dying weeks later. The doctors have modern drugs but admit they cannot identify the illness, so they cannot treat it. He gives it a placeholder name, Disease X, and his last dispatch notes that Japanese doctors are hoping the American scientists arriving on 11 September will know what to do.

fix.note: Still a thin cluster. No diarist here was aboard the Missouri. A British prisoner in Seoul records the signing as the moment he stopped being a POW, while Guerrero's undated postscript from these weeks describes custody with Axis diplomats at Atami. The ceremony is seen only at second hand, from the edges of Japan's former empire.

problem: 'Within hours his reports turned...' compresses the 8 and 9 September dispatches. 'Within days' is safer.

fix.bio: Weller slipped into southern Japan without permission and reached Nagasaki about four weeks after the bomb, before any other foreign reporter. His first dispatch defended the bombing. Within days his reports turned to hospital wards where people with no visible wounds were dying of an illness the doctors could not name.
